title: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
subtitle: Transitions · 35 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **35 of the official questions in Transitions are this one** — 20 Easy, 13 Medium, 2 Hard.
It is bottom-heavy, which makes it cheap points. Secure it early.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The earlier sentences give a constraint, need, principle or piece of evidence.
- The blank sentence describes an action someone took, an outcome or a conclusion that happens because of it.
- You can put 'so' between the sentences and it reads naturally.
- Choices mix one cause-effect word with contrast, example and time words.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Put 'so' or 'because of that' in the blank and read it aloud.
- 2) If it holds, pick the choice that means therefore: thus, hence, for this reason, consequently, as such.
- 3) If more than one cause word appears, use the one whose tone fits. 'As such' works when sentence two classifies what sentence one described.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You mix up 'an example of the principle' with 'the result of applying the principle'.
When sentence one states a general rule and sentence two shows someone using that rule to reach a finding, 'for example' looks right.
But the finding follows from the rule, so a cause-effect word is correct.
Also watch for decoys like 'consequently' when sentence two just corrects sentence one and doesn't follow from it.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You mix up 'an example of the principle' with 'the result of applying the principle'.
When sentence one states a general rule and sentence two shows someone using that rule to reach a finding, 'for example' looks right.
